options.name: P2MR
options.gloss: Pay to Merkle Root (BIP-360): the scriptPubKey commits to a Merkle root of leaf scripts, so no EC point is on chain before a spend

options.name: P2TRv2
options.gloss: Pay to Taproot v2: BIP-341 semantics plus PQC leaf types, an EC point on every output, ECC key path expected to be disabled later

options.name: P2TRH
options.gloss: Pay to Taproot Hash: like P2TRv2 but the scriptPubKey is a hash of the tweaked key and the key path uses public key recovery

options.name: P2QR
options.gloss: Pay to Quantum Resistant: the P2MR structure with all ECC opcodes disabled from the start

options.name: P2TRv2 plus CISA
options.gloss: P2TRv2 bundled with cross input signature aggregation as a single deployment

options.name: CISA output type
options.gloss: A standalone aggregation output type (BIP 460) deployed separately from the PQC work

options.name: Tripwire
options.gloss: An on chain proof of an ECDLP break automatically disables ECC spends inside the output type

options.name: Miner Lockdown
options.gloss: A hashrate majority trigger that disables ECC spends inside the output type

options.name: New witness style
options.gloss: An extra witness with its own discount and costing rules, needing a serialization and P2P change

options.name: Public Key Recovery
options.gloss: Spending without publishing the public key, saving about 32 bytes at the cost of a BIP-340 variant and of batch validation

options.name: Hybrid PQC opcodes
options.gloss: Opcodes that accept an ECC and a PQC signature together

options.name: Separate PQC leaf version
options.gloss: PQC opcodes confined to a leaf version that has no ECC opcodes

options.name: Upgrade hook
options.gloss: A dated anyone can spend deadline that forces a later consensus patch

options.name: CISA
options.gloss: Cross input signature aggregation itself, argued as a bundle or as a later separate step

options.name: SNARK signature aggregation
options.gloss: Post mine SNARK aggregation of signatures to curtail chain growth

options.name: SHRINCS
options.gloss: A hash based signature proposal not coupled to a block size increase

options.name: Half aggregation flow
options.gloss: Who aggregates signatures and where, signer side or relay side

options.name: Later CISA opt in flag
options.gloss: A pubkey grind bit or an extra output byte that lets a later CISA fork reuse the same witness version

options.name: Two stage deployment
options.gloss: A simple first output type now and a fuller one later

options.name: Extension block
options.gloss: A separate block area with its own UTXO set

options.name: Replay protection
options.gloss: Opt in replay protection shipped with the first SegWit v2

claims.quote: P2MR “Pay to Merkle Root” (BIP-360): The txout stores the Merkle root of a tree of leaf scripts.
claims.text: P2MR txouts store the Merkle root of a script tree, revealing the script and path at spend time without exposing EC points on-chain beforehand.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 “Pay to Taproot v2” (unclear origin): The exact same semantics as BIP-341 P2TR, but with PQC opcodes/leaf types added
claims.text: P2TRv2 retains BIP-341 semantics while adding PQC opcodes and leaf types, expecting a future soft fork to disable ECC within that output type.

claims.quote: P2TRH “Pay to Taproot Hash” (proposed here): Like P2TRv2, but the scriptPubKey contains a hash of the tweaked point Q.
claims.text: P2TRH hashes the tweaked point in the scriptPubKey and uses public key recovery for key path spending, matching P2TRv2 weight without pre-spend EC points.

claims.quote: P2QR “Pay to Quantum Resistant” (unclear origin): Identical to P2MR, but all ECC opcodes are disabled from the start.
claims.text: P2QR is identical to P2MR but disables ECC opcodes immediately, achieving unconditional quantum resistance at the cost of pre-quantum ECC efficiency.

claims.quote: Public Key Recovery (PKR) (proposed here): a special leaf version is added whose “script” is just an EC public key hash.
claims.text: Public Key Recovery saves approximately 32 bytes on spends by recovering the EC public key from the signature, but breaks batch validation.

claims.quote: New witness style (proposed here, discussed more here): this allows a new output type (or a new opcode) to access an additional witness extension to the transaction format
claims.text: A new witness style allows custom witness discounting rules for new output types but requires transaction serialization and P2P protocol changes.

claims.quote: Tripwire (proposed on ML): a proof for ECDLP breaking can be published on-chain, and this automatically disables ECC opcodes/keyspaths just within the output type itself.
claims.text: A tripwire mechanism automatically disables ECC functionality within an output type once a proof of ECDLP breaking is posted on-chain.

claims.quote: Miner lockdown (proposed on ML): a softfork signalling mechanism (e.g. BIP-9) is used, not for a separate softfork, but to let a hashrate majority trigger disabling of ECC opcodes/keypaths
claims.text: Miner lockdown allows a hashrate majority to trigger the disabling of ECC features within an output type without requiring ecosystem-wide softfork coordination.

claims.quote: Hybrid PQC opcodes (one scheme discussed here): instead of offering pure PQC opcodes/paths, have them accept hybrid ECC+PQC signatures.
claims.text: Hybrid PQC opcodes accept dual ECC and PQC signatures to protect against quantum scheme breaks, but increase signature size and verification cost.

claims.quote: Separate PQC leaf version (proposed on ML): restrict PQC opcodes to a separate leaf version which has no ECC opcodes.
claims.text: Restricting PQC opcodes to a dedicated leaf version avoids unexpected interactions with ECC disabling, but prevents user-defined hybrid scripts.

claims.quote: I believe the best solution is a combination of P2TRv2 and P2MR, covering distinct use cases.
claims.text: The optimal approach combines P2TRv2 for near-term adoption and P2MR for long-term migration.

claims.quote: To make “emergency” PQC available to as many users as possible: a P2TRv2 output type, with Tripwire and Miner Lockdown, and with a hash-based PQC signature opcode.
claims.text: Emergency PQC protection should be deployed via P2TRv2 with Tripwire, Miner Lockdown, and a hash-based PQC signature opcode.

claims.quote: I consider that dilemma an severe threat to Bitcoin (a more urgent one than CRQCs themselves even), because both options involve giving up a fundamental value proposition Bitcoin has.
claims.text: The steal-or-freeze dilemma is a more urgent threat to Bitcoin than quantum computers because both options compromise core value propositions.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 preserves the same fee profile as P2TR, avoiding “not migrating because it costs more”, and does not lose the P2TR incentives that brings.
claims.text: P2TRv2 avoids migration disincentives by retaining the exact fee profile and benefits of P2TR.

claims.quote: For developers/infrastructure, it is maximally close to today’s world, avoids the complexity of adding a new witness style or a new ECC signature scheme.
claims.text: P2TRv2 minimizes developer complexity by avoiding new witness styles or new ECC signature schemes.

claims.quote: It is compatible with most/all workflows I’m familiar with, including xpub/descriptor sharing
claims.text: P2TRv2 maintains compatibility with standard wallet workflows, including xpub and descriptor sharing.

claims.quote: No P2MR or P2TRH. These add additional complexity, cost, or both, to users that may stifle adoption
claims.text: Using P2MR or P2TRH for initial emergency migration adds complexity and cost that would hinder widespread adoption.

claims.quote: The actual automatic ECC-disabling mechanisms (especially Miner Lockdown) that may be more bikeshed-prone could be introduced later when/if CRQC threats are closer.
claims.text: Controversial automated ECC-disabling mechanisms like Miner Lockdown can be deferred until quantum threats are nearer.

claims.quote: To prepare for longer-term full migration, a P2MR-based output type, with Tripwire and Miner Lockdown as well, plus a new witness style to give its ECC usage the same fee structure as P2TR.
claims.text: Long-term post-quantum migration should use P2MR with Tripwire, Miner Lockdown, and a new witness style matching P2TR fees.

claims.quote: No more P2TR variants, to avoid the overhead/complexity of a privileged ECC-only path which is useless in a post-ECC world.
claims.text: Long-term output designs should avoid P2TR variants because a privileged ECC path provides no value in a post-ECC environment.

claims.quote: given that PKR verification is (slightly) slower than normal ECC verification, I don’t think it’s unreasonable to just use normal BIP-340 for ECC instead
claims.text: Standard BIP-340 with cost discounting is preferable to public key recovery in P2MR due to PKR's slower verification.

claims.quote: All continued use of ECC in the face of rising CRQC probability relies on some entities making the call as to when ECC is to be considered vulnerable
claims.text: All ECC-based transitional schemes fundamentally depend on specific entities deciding when ECC has become compromised.

claims.quote: The P2MR witness comes out 32 bytes lighter than the equivalent P2TR script path spend at every depth (except m = 7, where the control blocks fall on opposite sides of a compact size boundary and it i
claims.text: P2MR witnesses are generally 32 bytes lighter than equivalent P2TR script path spends.

claims.quote: P2MR effectively gets one extra tree level for the price of a P2TR script path.
claims.text: P2MR accommodates an additional Merkle tree depth for the same witness cost as a P2TR script path.

claims.quote: The consensus delta for P2MR as specified is ~96 lines on top of Core’s existing taproot machinery, because witness v2 reuses tapscript execution, the BIP-342 sighash and the Merkle walk unchanged
claims.text: P2MR requires minimal consensus changes to Bitcoin Core because it reuses existing Taproot execution and sighash logic.

claims.quote: Of the types listed, P2MR (and P2QR, which shares its structure) is the only one that is nearly free to implement given taproot; P2TRH and PKR need a BIP-340 variant
claims.text: P2MR and P2QR have lower implementation complexity than alternatives like P2TRH and PKR that require BIP-340 variants.

claims.quote: Bombs are the activation of something, not the stabilisation of that thing. QCs require control, not release; they are not bombs.
claims.text: Comparing quantum computing development to nuclear bomb development is flawed because quantum computing requires precise control and stabilization rather than explosive release.

claims.quote: So if you’re going to compare with nuclear you have to argue it’s more like fission reactors (that were created within a span of years) than fusion reactors
claims.text: A nuclear analogy for quantum computing should debate whether its development timeline resembles quickly built fission reactors or long-delayed fusion reactors.

claims.quote: CISA provides a natural vessel for P2TRv2 which is asymptotically (as the number of outputs inputs grows) so efficient as to only require 1 byte witnesses for full-agg EC spends.
claims.text: CISA enables P2TRv2 to asymptotically require only a 1-byte witness per input for fully aggregated elliptic-curve spends.

claims.quote: like P2TRv2, CISA’s output type requires we post bare EC pubkeys on-chain in the SPK and so it has the same PQ-security profile as P2TRv2.
claims.text: CISA's output type requires publishing bare EC public keys in the scriptPubKey, giving it the same post-quantum security profile as P2TRv2.

claims.quote: This would lower P2MR’s asymptotic per-input EC spend cost from 96 bytes (with PKR), but only to 64 bytes (with CISA), almost at par with P2TR today.
claims.text: Using CISA with P2MR lowers the asymptotic per-input EC spend cost to 64 bytes compared to 96 bytes with public-key recovery.

claims.quote: This trick works for P2TRH as well, with asymptotic EC witness weight reduced to 32 bytes per input (just one pubkey per full-agg output).
claims.text: CISA can reduce the asymptotic EC witness weight for P2TRH to 32 bytes per input.

claims.quote: With CISA, disabling ECC and switching to PQC is now even more expensive than it would’ve been without CISA.
claims.text: Deploying CISA increases the economic cost and user disruption of eventually disabling ECC in favor of post-quantum cryptography.

claims.quote: this would allow us to aggregate thousands of hash-based signatures across a whole block into one succinct (few hundred KB) proof
claims.text: PQ-SNARK aggregation could compress thousands of hash-based signatures across an entire block into a single succinct proof.

claims.quote: Flock can prove validation of hundreds of such signatures per second, especially when parallelized.
claims.text: The Flock SNARK system is capable of proving validation for hundreds of hash-based signatures per second.

claims.quote: There are two hurdles to overcome when getting users to adopt new output types:
claims.text: Adopting new output types requires overcoming the hurdles of software/infrastructure availability and user demand.

claims.quote: In my view, (1) is unlikely to be influenced significantly by feerate gains (IIRC CISA has a max WU reduction of ~28%, and only for extreme many-inputs few-outputs transactions)
claims.text: Feerate reductions from CISA are unlikely to significantly accelerate developer and infrastructure adoption outside of a sustained high-fee environment.

claims.quote: Rather, I think the converse effect is more relevant: users may not want to adopt things that increase cost. This is why I argued against (pure) P2MR before.
claims.text: User adoption is bottlenecked more by aversion to cost increases than driven by minor potential fee savings.

claims.quote: On the other hand, (1) is likely influenced significantly by implementation complexity, and CISA does add to that.
claims.text: Software implementation and ecosystem adoption are hindered by added complexity, which CISA introduces.

claims.quote: adding CISA to the mix may be a net negative for the goal of getting the long tail to adopt PQC, due to more complexity in getting the output type spec’ed and softforked in
claims.text: Combining CISA with PQC proposals could hinder broad PQC adoption by increasing specification and softfork complexity with minimal adoption incentive gains.

claims.quote: In a post-CRQC world, we likely need to move away further from witness-serialized-size as resource limiting metric, and give more relative weight to computation
claims.text: Post-quantum algorithms like hash-based signatures require resource limits to shift weight from serialized witness size toward computation.

claims.quote: if the differentiation becomes that P2MR is more for the longer term, it does make sense to have it there from the beginning even if that delays P2MR somewhat.
claims.text: If P2MR serves as a long-term post-quantum solution, it should incorporate new witness styles from the start despite the added deployment delay.

claims.quote: CISA isn’t so complex to implement locally, e.g. for single-signer wallets.
claims.text: Cross-input signature aggregation is not overly complex to implement in local single-signer wallet setups.

claims.quote: even if devs don’t want to invest the time up-front in doing even the most rudimentary (half) aggregation, they could still very easily deploy the CISA output type using non-aggregated BIP340 signatur
claims.text: Wallets can adopt CISA output types initially using standard non-aggregated BIP-340 signatures without implementing signature aggregation upfront.

claims.quote: Adding half or full aggregation later is as simple as a software update without any user-action needed
claims.text: Wallets can enable half or full signature aggregation later via software updates without requiring action from users.

claims.quote: Verification costs are a one-time cost per-node, but storage costs for archival nodes are eternal.
claims.text: Computational verification is a one-time expense per node, whereas archival storage costs accumulate permanently over time.

claims.quote: A block size increase of the magnitude needed to make even the smallest (XMSS) hash-based sigs fee-competitive with ECC would be an 8 fold increase (4mb → 32mb per block) at least
claims.text: Making hash-based signatures fee-competitive with elliptic curve cryptography would require at least an 8-fold increase in block size.

claims.quote: to increase the block size, we must also allow retroactive aggregation of signatures (or blocks) via SNARKs to curtail chain growth
claims.text: Increasing block size should be paired with retroactive SNARK-based signature or block aggregation to control archival chain growth.

claims.quote: With SHRINCS we have not coupled our proposal to a blocksize increase - at least, not initially.
claims.text: The initial SHRINCS proposal avoids requiring a controversial block size limit increase.

claims.quote: I agree the bandwidth cost must be accounted for somehow even in the best case scenario where signatures can be aggregated block-wide with zero cost by miners.
claims.text: Transaction relay bandwidth costs must still be accounted for even if miners can aggregate signatures across an entire block for free.

claims.quote: For that long tail, I expect the bottleneck to be software/wallet/custodian support by existing providers, and with high probability in the relatively short term, I don’t think fee arguments will affe
claims.text: Long-tail PQC adoption will be bottlenecked by software and wallet support rather than driven by fee considerations in the short term.

claims.quote: I think adding CISA to the P2TRv2 bundle will increase the time it takes for P2TRv2 to become available, and that will likely reduce adoption before Q-day by the long tail more than fee incentives wil
claims.text: Bundling CISA into P2TRv2 will delay its readiness, reducing pre-Q-day adoption more than fee incentives would help.

claims.quote: If it’s not bundled with P2TRv2, it will need yet another output type, be bundled with P2MR, or not done at all.
claims.text: Omitting CISA from P2TRv2 means it must use a new output type, be bundled into P2MR, or be abandoned.

claims.quote: Post-Q-day, if hash-based PQC is adopted, I think the need for a different witness costing rule (and thus larger (pre-aggregated) serialized block sizes) is almost an inevitability
claims.text: Adopting hash-based PQC post-Q-day will inevitably require revising witness costing rules and increasing block sizes.

claims.quote: with cryptography that has a different CPU/size ratio, it seems inappropriate to only account for size.
claims.text: Cost formulas should not rely purely on size when new cryptography alters the balance between CPU validation and data size.

claims.quote: IMO, we will need a new witness extension if Q-day happens, and it seems reasonable to aim to have the technology ready for that before Q-day.
claims.text: A new witness extension will be needed if Q-day occurs, so the technology should be prepared in advance.

claims.quote: If we bundle CISA+P2TRv2 then P2TRv2 can’t deploy until CISA consensus validation rules are ready.
claims.text: Bundling CISA with P2TRv2 would delay P2TRv2 deployment until CISA consensus validation rules are finalized.

claims.quote: However I do think you underestimate the mass appeal of an output type with PQC support which is also the cheapest output type available.
claims.text: A post-quantum output type that is also the cheapest option would attract substantial adoption.

claims.quote: Recently i’ve also started thinking maybe we could do both: SNARK aggregation happening after blocks are mined, to assuage the long-term storage impact and make IBD faster.
claims.text: Applying SNARK aggregation after blocks are mined could alleviate long-term storage burdens and accelerate Initial Block Download.

claims.quote: Block-wide aggregation wouldn’t affect the efficiency of mempool transaction relay, so any costing adjustments that consider aggregation also have to keep TX relay in mind too.
claims.text: Costing changes that account for signature aggregation must also consider unaggregated mempool transaction relay bandwidth.

claims.quote: We can’t just fork in super huge signatures even if they have near zero verification cost. But we can try to strike a balance between performance and size.
claims.text: Signatures cannot be made arbitrarily large just because verification cost is low; size and validation performance must be balanced.

claims.quote: Therefore we could justify putting 16x more signature bytes into a block and still incur roughly same CPU cost during signature validation.
claims.text: Lower verification cost per byte in SHRINCS allows for more signature bytes per block without increasing signature validation CPU load relative to Schnorr.

claims.quote: Stateful signatures can be made even cheaper.
claims.text: Stateful hash-based signatures can offer even lower per-byte verification costs than stateless schemes.

claims.quote: The 246/10 approach described there has you divide nodes into 246 groups, each storing 10% of total blockchain data, and you need to connect to (at least) 10 peers from distinct groups
claims.text: The 246/10 fountain coding approach requires connecting to at least 10 peers from distinct groups rather than any arbitrary combination of 10 peers.

claims.quote: The two aggregation scheme BIPs (458, 459) as well as the CISA BIP 460 have had a few eyes on them. More would be better, of course, but as far as I am concerned they are complete with reference imple
claims.text: BIPs 458, 459, and 460 are functionally complete with reference implementations and extensive test vectors.

claims.quote: Review of the secp256k1 implementations is probably the biggest lift looking at how long Silent Payments took. I consider this the primary blocker in terms of implementation.
claims.text: Reviewing the secp256k1 pull requests for BIP 458 and 459 is the main implementation blocker for CISA.

claims.quote: This new version of BIP 460 that makes opted-out inputs plain BIP 341 key path spends
claims.text: A revised BIP 460 specifies that opted-out inputs use standard BIP 341 key path spends.

claims.quote: What this should do is take wallet adoption out of the equation since there is no need for them to adopt any new signing logic.
claims.text: Using plain BIP 341 key path spends for CISA opt-outs prevents wallet adoption delays since wallets require no immediate signing logic changes.

claims.quote: In terms of technical implementation and review I think CISA is currently far ahead of whatever the PQ part of P2TRv2 would look like.
claims.text: CISA's technical implementation and specification are substantially more mature than the post-quantum components for P2TRv2.

claims.quote: On secp256k1 for example, where resources have been very scarce for a while, a group of new people are contributing and reviewing and afaik none of them are working on hash-based PQ stuff in parallel
claims.text: Reviewers working on secp256k1 do not appear to significantly overlap with researchers developing hash-based post-quantum signature implementations.

claims.quote: I think that offering benefits for the case that CRQCs are delayed or never happen should help to form community consensus much faster
claims.text: Including CISA helps build consensus by providing non-PQ benefits in case cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers are delayed.

claims.quote: If there is a speed-up happening it is relatively easy to drop the CISA part from the soft fork that is in development.
claims.text: CISA could easily be removed from a proposed soft fork bundle if quantum computing progress accelerates unexpectedly.

claims.quote: we’re five years in, have seen multiple periods of mempool congestion in that time (some taking months), and not even all providers support sending to it, let alone use it as default for new addresses
claims.text: Despite years of mempool congestion, Taproot adoption remains low across providers for sending and address defaults.

claims.quote: Full-agg CISA can improve over P2TR more than P2TR did over P2WPH, but only for sufficiently complex transactions.
claims.text: Full-aggregation CISA yields higher relative vsize savings than Taproot did over SegWit, but only for sufficiently complex transactions.

claims.quote: adopting workflows that allow such transactions is an even bigger task than adding PQC as it will typically involve adding interactivity
claims.text: Adopting workflows that leverage CISA requires adding interactivity, making it a harder task than introducing post-quantum cryptography.

claims.quote: An extension block, as discussed years ago as a scalability proposal, is something very different and much more invasive than what we’re talking about here.
claims.text: An extension block proposal is far more invasive than adding a new witness area for post-quantum signatures.

claims.quote: I am just talking about a new witness in transaction serialization, like Segwit did, and the design discussed here is somewhat less invasive than that even
claims.text: The proposed approach relies on a new serialization witness, making it even less invasive than SegWit.

claims.quote: it’s very unlikely it’ll have the same size/verification characteristics as ECC, even if it’s not as extreme as hash-based.
claims.text: Any post-quantum cryptographic scheme is unlikely to match the size and verification efficiency of elliptic-curve cryptography.

claims.quote: The big one is block propagation speed: practically, minimizing the time between a miner finding a block, getting it across the network, up to the point where other miners can start hashing on top of
claims.text: The primary performance metric of concern is block propagation speed between miners.

claims.quote: single sig: taproot is very slightly more expensive than p2wpkh due to the larger output
claims.text: For single-signature transactions, Taproot is slightly more expensive than P2WPKH because of its larger output size.

claims.quote: n-of-n multisig: wasn’t more efficient until musig became available
claims.text: N-of-n multisig transactions did not become more efficient under Taproot until MuSig implementation became available.

claims.quote: k-of-n multisig: we’ve got FROSTsnap signing devices, but as I understand it we don’t have a spec/standard for FROST yet
claims.text: A standard specification for FROST is not yet available, despite the existence of FROST-based signing devices.

claims.quote: afaik in practice we don’t have any complicated enough scripts in common use (ie, not “new features/tech stacks/stupid hype stuff”) that they would be significantly cheaper with taproot
claims.text: There are practically no widely used complex scripts that would achieve significant fee savings from Taproot.

claims.quote: So I’d say the timeframe for fee-driven adoption of taproot has only been at most 6 months (for n-of-n; still waiting for k-of-n), and that’s been in a time of record low fee levels.
claims.text: The opportunity for fee-incentivized Taproot adoption has only existed for at most six months and occurred during a period of historically low fees.

claims.quote: I think for exchanges it could be significant – maybe reducing tx fees by 30% for larger consolidation txs; perhaps 60% if you got to switch from CHECKMULTISIG to FROST key path sigs at the same time.
claims.text: Cross-input signature aggregation could reduce consolidation transaction fees for exchanges by roughly 30%, or up to 60% when paired with FROST key path signatures.

claims.quote: I think you want a relatively high chance of collisions because the set of nodes you collide with is also your anonymity set as a node
claims.text: A higher collision rate is desirable because colliding nodes constitute the node's anonymity set.

claims.quote: I think aiming for roughly the same signature verificiation as BIP-340 seems like a reasonable rule of thumb.
claims.text: Aiming for post-quantum signature verification costs roughly comparable to BIP-340 Schnorr signatures is a sensible baseline.

claims.quote: 8MB blocks with w=64 seems almost appealing
claims.text: Using 8MB blocks with parameter w=64 is an appealing configuration for balancing post-quantum signature cost and size.

claims.quote: would probably require new p2p messages for chunking blocks or something though.
claims.text: Adopting 8MB blocks would likely necessitate new peer-to-peer messages for transmitting chunked blocks.

claims.quote: I think it’s unlikely that the prisoner’s dilemma played much of a role here. Senders were/are (almost completely) willing to send to P2WSH already, with a similar per-output cost as P2TR.
claims.text: The prisoner's dilemma likely did not hinder Taproot adoption because senders were already willing to pay comparable output costs for P2WSH.

claims.quote: A more plausible explanation is that receivers didn’t want a different output type for change and for receiving, and that P2TR for both combined didn’t seem sufficiently beneficial
claims.text: Taproot adoption lagged because users disliked mixing address types for change and receives, or did not see enough fee benefit overall.

claims.quote: Some limit is necessary for verifiable chunking of blocks
claims.text: Verifiable block chunking requires a per-transaction limit to guarantee feasibility.

claims.quote: But a tx weight limit might not be a bad thing in general (from a block template optimization perspective).
claims.text: A general transaction weight limit could aid block template optimization.

claims.quote: I tend to agree with Pieter that it’s somehow slightly ‘off’ to merge CISA into this. CISA, I agree, does not have nearly as big of a selling point in practice as some people want to believe.
claims.text: Merging CISA into a post-quantum proposal is ill-advised because CISA's practical utility is limited.

claims.quote: It would be better to have it available as a “here’s an output type that will be cheaper for your ordinary wallet when it matters, which is to say, when you have to consolidate a bunch of utxos”
claims.text: CISA should be positioned simply as an output type providing modest savings during UTXO consolidation.

claims.quote: people are slow to switch and reluctant to switch unless they see a reason, which is either, cheaper fees or “there’s a big chunk of the ecosystem using it”.
claims.text: Ecosystem adoption of new output types requires either clear fee savings or widespread network momentum.

claims.quote: The whole coinjoin/batching etc. etc. angle is going to remain niche unless something big changes.
claims.text: CoinJoin and batching use cases for CISA are likely to remain niche.

claims.quote: And it would be nice if they didn’t have to overlay another technical decision on top of it (quantum stuff).
claims.text: Adoption of CISA should not be coupled with post-quantum cryptography transitions.

claims.quote: AI has made making such changes a lot faster, cheaper and (arguably) safer, especially when there is a spec that you can point the bots to.
claims.text: AI tools reduce the cost and technical barriers for understaffed projects to implement new protocol upgrades.

claims.quote: Apathy of users to move coins and general disbelief in CRCQs happening are where I see the bigger issues.
claims.text: The primary obstacle to post-quantum adoption is user apathy and doubt regarding CRQCs rather than wallet implementation difficulties.

claims.quote: We currently don’t think that implementing fullagg in Payjoin requires additional communication rounds but we will confirm it with a PoC soon
claims.text: Full-aggregation CISA in Payjoin is expected not to require extra communication rounds.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 + PQC + CISA could be implemented and used without CISA (only use plain BIP341 opted-out) or without PQC (not implementing the required paths).
claims.text: A combined P2TRv2 proposal allows implementations to selectively adopt PQC or CISA independently based on their resources.

claims.quote: reaching all self-custodial users and motivating them to move their funds is the harder part, even when their favorite wallet already has released an upgrade that supports the new output type.
claims.text: Motivating self-custodial users to migrate funds to a new output type is harder than getting custodial services to adopt it.

claims.quote: This is why I think bundling would help PQC adoption in many possible scenarios. It makes the pill not as bitter and gives the doubters a reason to still be interested in the change.
claims.text: Bundling CISA with PQC incentivizes adoption among people who remain skeptical of quantum threats.

claims.quote: for those that don’t see it as a danger (yet) the messaging matters much more and it may be better for them to hear “efficiency upgrade with PQC included just in case CRQCs do happen”.
claims.text: Positioning the proposal as an efficiency upgrade that includes PQC as a contingency improves reception among quantum skeptics.

claims.quote: As CRQCs appear to get closer and migration takes action demand for block space will rise necessarily.
claims.text: Migrating to quantum-resistant outputs will significantly increase block space demand, making aggregation optimizations especially valuable.

claims.quote: Having a P2TRv2 with PQC and another P2TRv3 with CISA seems to be worse for adoption in my mind.
claims.text: Splitting PQC and CISA into two separate output types would result in worse adoption than combining them.

claims.quote: I do see the P2TRv2 with an ulterior disablement of ECC spends within the output type itself as a reasonable path forward.
claims.text: P2TRv2 with a built-in future disablement of ECC spends is a reasonable approach to prepare for quantum threats.

claims.quote: The fact it’s happening with the clear design goal of a potential future disablement means that users have voluntary opted-in by sending their funds to the new P2TRv2
claims.text: Users explicitly opt into potential future spend disablement by choosing to move funds into the new P2TRv2 output type.

claims.quote: designing a new dedicated output type with self-containing freezing effect avoid any uncertain future liability due to the retroactive effect the technical change would have
claims.text: Self-contained disablement rules in a dedicated output type avoid the liability and controversy of retroactively freezing non-consenting users' outputs.

claims.quote: We can introduce many leaves types where for the first one the ECC spend path would be disable when the disable flag event is reached and for the second one the ECC spend path is not disabled
claims.text: P2TRv2 could support leaf types that selectively disable or preserve ECC spending paths upon a trigger flag.

claims.quote: We can introduce different class of flag events for the spend by using some space bit flags in the leaves versioning itself to say if the user commits to the effect of Tripwire or the effect of Miner
claims.text: Leaf versioning bit flags could allow users to specify which disablement trigger mechanism (e.g., Tripwire or Miner Lockdown) applies to their output.

claims.quote: About the idea bundling P2TRv2 with CISA, I would rather suggest a no.
claims.text: P2TRv2 should not be bundled with CISA because CISA is an optimization rather than a response to an urgent critical security threat.

claims.quote: all the post-quantum changes for an eventual P2TRv2 are going to be a novel stack of complexity for them already
claims.text: Hardware wallets already face implementation challenges and adding P2TRv2 post-quantum changes will introduce significant new complexity.

claims.quote: Quantum-resistance is the greater selling point, which is why i think P2MR is still the best option on the table.
claims.text: Quantum resistance is a stronger motivation than CISA, making P2MR the top proposal.

claims.quote: it gives devs a reason to migrate without committing them to any up-front work supporting CISA. Supporting PQC will be far more challenging by comparison.
claims.text: P2TRv2 bundled with CISA incentivizes developer migration without requiring upfront CISA integration work, which is much simpler than supporting PQC.

claims.quote: Without CISA, we might as well do P2MR. Then at least we can correctly claim we have deployed a quantum secure output type, and shame wallets who don’t migrate.
claims.text: If CISA is excluded, deploying P2MR is preferable because it provides an unequivocally quantum-secure output format.

claims.quote: With CISA, users can at least plead “this new address format is cheaper AND has a quantum migration path, you should support it or i’m going elsewhere.”
claims.text: Combining CISA with P2TRv2 gives users an immediate fee incentive alongside a quantum migration path to pressure wallet support.

claims.quote: By bundling PQC with an ECC optimization, we can simultaneously please the quantum bears and the quantum bulls in one self-consistent package.
claims.text: Bundling post-quantum cryptography with elliptic curve optimization satisfies both quantum skeptics and quantum believers in a single proposal.

claims.quote: FWIW this would implicitly cap the number of inputs in a transaction, depending on signature size, and would mean some large multisignature scripts would be completely unspendable.
claims.text: A transaction size cap would limit input counts depending on signature size and render some large multisig scripts unspendable.

claims.quote: with 5kb signatures (as proposed in SHRINCS’ current stateless parameter set), a 100kb TX size cap would mean less than 20 inputs per transaction.
claims.text: A 100 kB transaction limit with 5 kB signatures would restrict transactions to fewer than 20 inputs.

claims.quote: Measuring in weight units seems more reasonable if you assume the PQ signatures have a discount.
claims.text: Limiting transaction capacity via weight units is more appropriate if post-quantum signatures receive a witness discount.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 by itself does not address the critical security risk (ECDLP being broken). The critical security risks are only addressed after EC is disabled.
claims.text: P2TRv2 alone does not eliminate ECDLP vulnerability until elliptic curve spending paths are explicitly deactivated.

claims.quote: All a wallet has to do to support CISA key-spending (opt-out path) now is to bump their witness version. This is exactly the same level of integration difficulty as stock P2TRv2 (without CISA)
claims.text: CISA's opt-out design means wallets only need to bump their witness version, matching the integration difficulty of baseline P2TRv2.

claims.quote: The complexity added by CISA is then mainly on the consensus validation side, which compared to PQ signature validation is minor IMO.
claims.text: Consensus validation complexity added by CISA is minor compared to that of post-quantum signature verification.

claims.quote: Whatever output type we deploy will need to come with new wallet standards for how to derive PQ keys securely
claims.text: Any deployed post-quantum output type will require new wallet standards for secure key derivation.

claims.quote: shifting away from BIP32 and towards some entirely new multi-algorithm HD wallet standard that nobody has even defined yet
claims.text: Supporting P2TRv2 requires wallets to abandon BIP32 in favor of an undefined multi-algorithm HD wallet standard.

claims.quote: Wallets will also need to implement the PQ key generation algorithms, and probably test that against static test vectors
claims.text: Wallets must implement post-quantum key generation algorithms and validate them against static test vectors.

claims.quote: Simply “bumping the witness version” is insufficient even for P2TRv2, with or without CISA
claims.text: Simply bumping the witness version does not make P2TRv2 an easy upgrade for wallets.

claims.quote: Where I can be skeptical, it’s on the wallet and node complexity changes required to support CISA in itself.
claims.text: The wallet and node complexity required to implement CISA raises technical skepticism.

claims.quote: it does sounds to me technically possible to introduce discount for a future post-quantum scheme by introducing a novel witness scheme at the same time.
claims.text: A novel witness scheme could technically introduce weight discounts for future post-quantum schemes as an alternative to CISA.

claims.quote: The BIPs say nothing about how it would be done in practice, if it would be done by the wallets only, with not special support from network full-node, or that for half-aggregation we would have magic
claims.text: CISA BIPs lack practical details on whether aggregation occurs exclusively via wallets or requires node/mempool aggregation logic.

claims.quote: This approach has been done naively in the past on some cryptocurrencies e.g Mimblewimble and it was the source of subtle privacy deanonymization attacks
claims.text: Naive in-mempool aggregation has historically introduced subtle deanonymization vulnerabilities in other cryptocurrencies like Mimblewimble.

claims.quote: realistically for post quantum changes we might need multiple soft fork changes spread on multiple years, to make the Bitcoin network as robust as we can.
claims.text: Achieving quantum robustness for Bitcoin will likely require multiple soft forks deployed over several years.

claims.quote: the change in itself is for pure privacy and performance reason, and in my subjective scale of value, I’m not ranking it as importantly than soft-fork changes justified for network security.
claims.text: Changes for privacy and performance like CISA have lower priority than soft forks directly addressing network security risks.

claims.quote: in pure terms of social dynamics one we should keep the technical surface as much reduced as we can for post-quantum change.
claims.text: The technical scope of post-quantum consensus changes should be kept minimal given exogenous timeline pressures.

claims.quote: My main view is simply that CISA won’t help adoption, and is thus not worth the additional complexity of consensus changes.
claims.text: CISA is unlikely to drive adoption and therefore does not warrant the added complexity of a consensus change.

claims.quote: Neither P2TRv2 nor P2MR are a “quantum secure output type” in an absolute sense.
claims.text: Neither P2TRv2 nor P2MR is absolutely quantum-secure since any ongoing reliance on ECC depends on timely protocol-level intervention.

claims.quote: I believe that it is a practical impossibility for many software and users to adopt workflows in which P2MR provides quantum-resistance, due to ingrained use of public key sharing.
claims.text: Existing key-sharing practices make it practically impossible for most wallet software and users to achieve quantum resistance under P2MR.

claims.quote: Our goal as protocol designers is not to be able to claim we did enough by providing people a good option. Our goal is trying to design something people will actually use correctly.
claims.text: Protocol design should aim for solutions that users can realistically adopt and use correctly rather than technically optimal options they will misuse.

claims.quote: people may choose to adopt it in an “unprepared” way (without PQC path) because the output type has advantages beyond quantum protection.
claims.text: Adding non-quantum benefits like CISA may cause users to adopt the new output type without configuring quantum fallback paths.

claims.quote: I think there should be at least one in the initial deployment, to set a clear expectation.
claims.text: At least one automatic ECC-disabling mechanism should be included in the initial deployment to establish clear expectations.

claims.quote: A tripwire is probably the best choice. Although it can be bikeshed, it can’t be gamed. Only a serious problem with classic cryptography (or an implementation bug) can trigger it prematurely.
claims.text: A cryptographic tripwire cannot be gamed and will only trigger prematurely if classical cryptography breaks or an implementation bug occurs.

claims.quote: The reason to do it from the start, is because hitch-hiking with a new SegWit version offers the largest possible design space.
claims.text: Replay protection should be designed from the start because coupling it with a new SegWit version provides the greatest design flexibility.

claims.quote: From a user-experience point of view, once their wallet adopts CISA, it can gradually migrate coins over to it, in a way that’s not noticeable / distracting.
claims.text: Soft-forking CISA into SegWit v2 later allows wallets to migrate coins smoothly without disruptive UX changes.

claims.quote: And of course the anonymity set doesn’t need to splinter again.
claims.text: Enabling CISA via a soft fork in the same SegWit version prevents splintering the anonymity set into another output version.

claims.quote: we could allocate 1 bit of the public key to mark it anyone-can-spend, with the later CISA fork using that as the opt-in all wallets set it by default (regardless of support).
claims.text: A pubkey bit could be reserved as an anyone-can-spend marker that a future CISA soft fork repurposes as an opt-in flag.

claims.quote: Neither helps with the anonymity set , and moving forward such a flag would likely reveal wallet capability.
claims.text: Using explicit pubkey flag bits does not preserve the anonymity set and tends to leak wallet capabilities.

claims.quote: It’s about why the first output type (the P2TRv2 one) does not use P2MR or P2TRH. The later output type can use P2MR or P2QR.
claims.text: The initial P2TRv2 output type avoids P2MR or P2TRH, whereas a later output type could adopt P2MR or P2QR.

claims.quote: If it needs to cover key path spends (which is the most interesting application), it needs a separate output type.
claims.text: Enabling CISA for key path spends requires a separate output type rather than soft-forking it into SegWit v2 later.

claims.quote: That makes it, for all intents and purposes, a separate output type. Just one that shares the same witness version.
claims.text: Allocating a public key bit to signal anyone-can-spend effectively creates a separate output type under the same witness version.

claims.quote: It boils down to a way to add segwit subversions.
claims.text: The discussed approach effectively functions as a mechanism to introduce SegWit subversions.

claims.quote: Either at the expense of making every output 1 byte larger, or extra complexity due to having to grind an extra bit. Neither is hugely appealing.
claims.text: Adding SegWit subversions involves undesirable trade-offs: either increasing output size by one byte or introducing complexity through bit grinding.

claims.quote: I think that’s a bad idea, because it’d be unsafe to use due to the risk of later confiscation via tripwire.
claims.text: A naked P2TRv2 deployment is unsafe because it leaves funds vulnerable to later confiscation via tripwires.

claims.quote: I believe half and full agg should be done by signers, either interactively (full agg) or non-interactively (half agg). I don’t believe relay nodes are expected to do any half-aggregation themselves.
claims.text: Signature aggregation should be executed by signers rather than network relay nodes.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 is easy to use “correctly” but even with correct usage your coins are not necessarily safe. With P2MR, perfectly “correct” usage is harder, but has meaningful impact on security.
claims.text: Correct usage of P2TRv2 does not guarantee coin safety, whereas proper P2MR usage provides meaningful security benefits.

claims.quote: if i just use a regular single-signer phone or desktop wallet, all my wallet has to do is (1) not reuse addresses and (2) not transmit my xpubs off-site.
claims.text: Single-signer wallets can maintain quantum resistance under P2MR simply by avoiding address reuse and keeping xpubs local.

claims.quote: however “leaky” P2MR is or isn’t when put into practice, P2TRv2 will be at least as leaky and almost certainly worse, because 100% of P2TRv2 EC keys are exposed from the get-go.
claims.text: P2TRv2 is inherently leakier to quantum attacks than P2MR because it reveals all EC public keys upfront.

claims.quote: Without CISA though, the efficiency gap between P2MR and P2TR is tiny: smaller than the gap between P2WPKH and P2TR
claims.text: Without CISA, the difference in efficiency between P2MR and P2TR is smaller than that between P2WPKH and P2TR.

claims.quote: With @fjahr’s CISA or @starius’ EC recovery implemented on top of P2MR, then P2MR is actually more efficient than P2WPKH which is what most retail wallets are using today.
claims.text: Adding CISA or EC recovery to P2MR makes it more fee-efficient than standard P2WPKH.

claims.quote: Because they’re two radically different proposals with radically different motivations, that’s all I meant.
claims.text: PQC and CISA are fundamentally distinct proposals serving different motivations.

claims.quote: sometimes the way you put the pieces together has unexpected side effects. Homomorphic commitments to amounts is balance preserving, mathematically, but that doesn’t mean you don’t introduce risk fact
claims.text: Combining technically orthogonal cryptographic concepts in practice can introduce unexpected real-world side effects or risk factors.

claims.quote: Some people would want a CISA soft fork, but not the PQC one (or want a different PQC one). They might be orthogonal elements of a proposal on paper, but might not be in practice.
claims.text: Different stakeholders may favor CISA without wanting PQC or vice versa, meaning they may not be orthogonal in practice.

claims.quote: Indeed, it would/will be more complicated to do separate changes instead of combined ones. I don’t think that should affect choices about proposals though.
claims.text: The added complexity of deploying separate changes rather than a bundled one should not dictate proposal choices.

claims.quote: the BIP specifies how signers produce their signatures and how those get combined, but it does not make rules about who runs the combining step
claims.text: The BIP defines signature production and combination procedures without dictating which party executes the combining step.

claims.quote: Half-agg is explicitly opt-in, each signer commits to the aggregation mode already in its signature message, so a node could only ever aggregate signatures whose creators already chose to aggregate
claims.text: Half-aggregation is strictly opt-in because signers commit to the aggregation mode directly in their signature messages.

claims.quote: the s-values of the individual signatures never appear in the actual transaction, a member witness only carries the nonce share
claims.text: Individual s-values are omitted from the final transaction witness, which only includes nonce shares.

claims.quote: To do anything, nodes would have to receive the full signatures through this new P2P protocol and the mempool would need to accept and hold transactions that are not valid yet
claims.text: Node-level aggregation would require new P2P protocols for transmitting full signatures and mempool handling of incomplete transactions.

claims.quote: Here aggregation is within one transaction and happens before broadcast
claims.text: Unlike Mimblewimble cut-through during relay, this aggregation occurs intra-transaction prior to broadcasting.

claims.quote: Broadcast middleware that aggregates would need the full signatures handed to it out of band, e.g. in PSBT fields, since they are not in the transaction as explained above
claims.text: Third-party broadcast aggregating middleware requires full signatures to be supplied out of band.

claims.quote: You cannot expect people to stop reusing addresses, because it doesn’t fall within the purview of software that protocol designers and developers control.
claims.text: Protocol designers cannot eliminate address reuse because it is driven by user behavior outside software control.

claims.quote: the only realistic way to avoid it is having everything and everyone move to a different layer (like Lightning’s BOLT11 invoices / BOLT12 payment codes) where the need for compatibility does not exist
claims.text: Eliminating address reuse realistically requires transitioning all users to alternative layers like Lightning invoices or payment codes.

claims.quote: I don’t think this is feasible in the timelines people are thinking of for CRQC, and probably needs decades.
claims.text: Migrating all Bitcoin users away from reusable on-chain addresses will likely take decades and cannot meet expected CRQC timelines.

claims.quote: This isn’t a software problem; it requires workflow/social changes and reimagining how people use Bitcoin.
claims.text: Preventing address reuse and off-site xpub leakage requires behavioral and workflow changes rather than purely software solutions.

claims.quote: Large amounts of keys cannot be reliably written on a piece of paper or a metal backup. They may not fit in a QR code. They may not fit on a tiny hardware screen for manual comparison.
claims.text: Managing large sets of preshared post-quantum keys creates practical usability and backup challenges for hardware wallets and offline storage.

claims.quote: I don’t consider that acceptable. You’re proposing an output type that, barring a future consensus change, automatically becomes insecure.
claims.text: Introducing an output type that automatically becomes insecure over time without a future hard/soft fork is unacceptable.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 and CISA pull in opposite directions. Not only in terms of features, but also in terms of expectations.
claims.text: P2TRv2 and CISA have conflicting technical features and user expectations.

claims.quote: I don’t think CRQC-skeptic CISA enthusiasts would accept an expectation that their EC spending path becomes unspendable before CRQCs materialize.
claims.text: CRQC skeptics who want CISA would likely reject an output type where the EC path is expected to be disabled.

claims.quote: it may be that the lack of CISA support hinders migration to P2TRv2.
claims.text: Failing to support CISA in P2TRv2 might slow down user adoption of P2TRv2.

claims.quote: P2TRv2 targets wallets / service providers different from those likely to adopt CISA.
claims.text: CISA and P2TRv2 target different user and wallet demographics.

claims.quote: So an argument for bundling the two would be to avoid this footprint.
claims.text: Bundling P2TRv2 and CISA would prevent distinguishable output types from fragmenting the anonymity set on-chain.

claims.quote: i too don’t expect the ~5% off for the vast majority of users to have much of an impact on the wallet developers’ decision to migrate to a new output type.
claims.text: A minor fee reduction of around 5% will not meaningfully motivate wallet developers to migrate to a new output format.

claims.quote: exchanges would migrate to it with or without CISA, because it’s already no more expensive and because it would keep them safe if/when CRQC risks materialize.
claims.text: Exchanges will adopt P2TRv2 regardless of CISA support because it incurs no additional cost and provides CRQC security.

claims.quote: Tripwire without miner lockdown is a non-binding constraint and as such does not really provide “teeth” to EC disabling, outside of a psychological effect
claims.text: Tripwire without miner lockdown lacks real enforcement power beyond establishing an expectation that EC paths will be disabled.

claims.quote: I think the major challenge with EC disabling is to prevent it from happening too soon.
claims.text: The primary risk with disabling elliptic curve spending paths is triggering the disablement prematurely.

claims.quote: Miner Lockdown, while it gives the collective of miners the ability to (i believe irrationally) trigger it prematurely, may help in reassuring those stakeholders who might otherwise push for an early
claims.text: Miner lockdown can reassure stakeholders concerned about unexpected quantum breakthroughs, even if miners could theoretically trigger it prematurely.

claims.quote: I think risk mitigation (P2TRv2 + Tripwire) and full migration (P2MR + eventual EC disabling + Witness style) should be provided in separate deployments.
claims.text: P2TRv2 risk mitigation and P2MR full migration should be deployed as separate soft forks.

claims.quote: the full migration path should only be made available once we have a higher degree of certainty that CRQCs will become a reality, while the risk mitigation should be provided regardless.
claims.text: Risk mitigation should deploy regardless of quantum certainty, whereas full migration should wait until CRQC reality is more certain.

claims.quote: Under these assumptions, why would you ever use the PQ spending path? That would make even today’s P2WSH “secure”. I don’t think that makes sense.
claims.text: The orange threat model assumptions render quantum-resistant spending paths unnecessary and do not make sense.

claims.quote: address reuse per se does not cause funds to have an exposed public key, only address reuse of an address that has previously been spent from does.
claims.text: Reusing an address only exposes its public key if that address was previously spent from.

claims.quote: P2TR and P2TRv2 are both clearly a regression from a PQ perspective compared to P2WPKH and other address types with hashed keys, until/unless ECC spending is disabled.
claims.text: P2TR and P2TRv2 are post-quantum regressions compared to P2WPKH and hashed-key addresses unless ECC spending is disabled.

claims.quote: moving such funds to P2MR rather than P2TRv2 would certainly feel less risky to someone who is informed about the potential threat of a CRQC.
claims.text: Informed users concerned about CRQCs would consider P2MR less risky than P2TRv2.

claims.quote: For the “taking payments” use case, it largely comes down to wallets and (especially) exchanges being excruciatingly slow to add support for sending to new address types.
claims.text: P2TR adoption for receiving payments has lagged due to very slow support from wallets and exchanges for new address formats.

claims.quote: Adding yet another address option to the mix would simply confuse end users who aren’t generally crypto-savvy.
claims.text: Introducing another address type causes confusion for non-technical end users.

claims.quote: For the “holding funds” use case, P2TR is more expensive for both one-input/two-output and two-input/two-output transactions, loses the inherent PQ resistance of P2WPKH, and has a much smaller anonymi
claims.text: For holding funds, P2TR is more expensive for common transaction sizes, loses P2WPKH's post-quantum resistance, and has a smaller anonymity set.

claims.quote: Adoption of P2TRv2 generally hinges on people trusting that the disabling triggers will work as intended, not too early and not too late, and that is the same for every user.
claims.text: Adoption of P2TRv2 depends across all users on trust that EC disabling triggers activate at the right time.

claims.quote: If the disabling triggers worked perfectly (only happens magically in the exact moment the first CRQC comes into existence), adopting P2TRv2 should be an absolute no-brainer
claims.text: P2TRv2 would be clearly preferable to alternative output types if disabling triggers could activate precisely when CRQCs emerge.

claims.quote: If people believe they are too risky, P2TRv2 likely won’t reach consensus in the first place, with or without CISA.
claims.text: P2TRv2 is unlikely to reach consensus if stakeholders view its disabling mechanisms as too risky.

claims.quote: I also don’t think these are the target audience for P2TRv2. If they’re properly managed they can migrate in time to a later P2MR output type too.
claims.text: Properly managed cold-storage users are not the target audience for P2TRv2 because they can migrate later to P2MR.

claims.quote: I recognize the psychological appeal of an output type that doesn’t have conditions attached (which is part of the reason for favoring also adding a later-stage P2MR output type
claims.text: The psychological appeal of unconditional quantum security supports eventually introducing a later P2MR output type alongside P2TRv2.

claims.quote: These things should be debated separately. Either the security of P2TRv2 is acceptable to the ecosystem, or not. And maybe adding CISA to it (or to P2MR) is a good idea, or not.
claims.text: The security acceptability of P2TRv2 and the merits of adding CISA are independent questions that should be debated separately.

claims.quote: All we can say for sure is that P2MR would protect some unknown fraction of coins from long-exposure attacks.
claims.text: P2MR protects an uncertain portion of coins against long-exposure quantum attacks.

claims.quote: First, workflow/social changes will be needed either way. If Q-day happens, it’d be a complete paradigm shift in the world of cryptography.
claims.text: Workflow and social changes are inevitable because quantum computing requires a complete cryptographic paradigm shift.

claims.quote: Second, this is a software problem. There are ways to do almost everything we’d need to, they’d just require some (reasonable) compromises.
claims.text: Mitigating quantum exposure risks can largely be solved in software through reasonable compromises.

claims.quote: i think PQ hardware wallet security under P2MR is completely doable.
claims.text: Hardware wallet post-quantum security is achievable under P2MR.

claims.quote: I believe CISA’s efficiency would significantly help move the needle on migration to a PQC-enabled address type
claims.text: CISA's efficiency improvements could meaningfully incentivize user migration to a post-quantum-enabled address format.

claims.quote: I believe that the benefits of P2TRv2 compared to P2MR (drop-in compat, 8vb efficiency gain) are negligible compared to the existential risk of all the P2TRv2 coins being exposed on Q-day.
claims.text: The minor efficiency and compatibility benefits of P2TRv2 are outweighed by the existential quantum exposure risk for those coins.

claims.quote: My stance is still that P2MR is the only truly post-quantum address format.
claims.text: P2MR is the only address format that is genuinely post-quantum secure.

questions.text: How can forward error correction (FEC) block storage sharding be coordinated robustly without a central directory?
What specific tip validation metrics are most critical, and does existing research document the impact of larger signatures on them?
Should individual transactions have a limit preventing them from including more than around 100kB of post-quantum signature data?
Why is it considered off or problematic to merge CISA into the P2TRv2 proposal?
Did BIP 54 have as many skilled reviewers and designers involved in its process as Taproot and Schnorr did?
Did sipa mean that P2MR should not be in the initial deployment, or was mentioning P2MR a typo?
Is it possible to design SegWit v2 so that CISA can be soft-forked in later without requiring another version bump?
Why would anyone use the post-quantum spending path under the assumptions of the orange threat model?
